content: In combinatorial mathematics, a block design, more formally known as a balanced incomplete block design (BIBD), is a specific type of set system. It has significant applications in experimental design, a branch of statistics, as well as in purely combinatorial studies. Consider a finite set ( X ), whose elements are referred to as points, and integers ( k ), ( r ), and ( lambda ), all greater than or equal to 1. A 2-design ( B ) is defined as a collection of ( k )-element subsets of ( X ), which are called blocks. The defining property of a 2-design is that the number ( r ) of blocks containing any given point ( x ) in ( X ) is constant, regardless of the choice of ( x ). Additionally, the number ( lambda ) of blocks that contain any pair of distinct points ( x ) and ( y ) in ( X ) is also constant, independent of the specific points chosen. The parameters of a block design are denoted as ( v ), ( b ), ( k ), ( r ), and ( lambda ). Here, ( v ) represents the total number of points in ( X ), ( b ) is the total number of blocks, ( k ) is the size of each block, ( r ) is the number of blocks containing any given point, and ( lambda ) is the number of blocks containing any given pair of points. Importantly, ( B ) does not necessarily include all possible ( k )-element subsets of ( X ), which is why the design is referred to as incomplete. Such a design is often described as a ( (v, k, lambda) )-design or, more fully, as a ( (v, b, r, k, lambda) )-design. The parameters ( v ), ( k ), and ( lambda ) are not independent of one another; they determine the values of ( b ) and ( r ), and not all combinations of ( v ), ( k ), and ( lambda ) are feasible. Examples of block designs include the lines in finite projective planes, where ( X ) is the set of points in the plane and ( lambda = 1 ). Another example is a Steiner triple system, where ( k = 3 ). Finite projective planes provide a relatively straightforward example of symmetric designs. A generalization of block designs is the concept of ( t )-designs. For any integer ( t geq 2 ), a ( t )-design ( B ) is a collection of ( k )-element subsets of ( X ), called blocks, such that the number ( r ) of blocks containing any given point ( x ) in ( X ) is constant, and the number ( lambda ) of blocks containing any specific ( t )-element subset ( T ) of ( X ) is also constant, independent of the choice of ( T ). The parameters of a ( t )-design are ( v ), ( b ), ( k ), ( r ), ( lambda ), and ( t ). Such a design is denoted as a ( t )-(v, k, ( lambda ))-design. As with 2-designs, the parameters ( v ), ( k ), ( lambda ), and ( t ) determine ( b ) and ( r ), and not all combinations of these parameters are possible. An example of a ( t )-design is the set of ( d )-dimensional subspaces in a finite projective geometry, where ( t = d + 1 ) and ( lambda = 1 ). It is worth noting that the term block design without further qualification typically refers to a 2-design.
